name: Desert Outpost
_background: Level 1 is fought on the layered desert-outpost set rather than a single image. The layers replace the
`background` key outright when present, so it is gone: see art/MODULAR_BACKGROUNDS.md for the pipeline and
art/layer_sets/desert_outpost.json for the build recipe that printed the block below.
Order is draw order, back to front, and the ground comes *before* the rock band rather than after it. The
rock stands on the basin floor, so the floor is painted first and the rock drawn onto it, exactly as a unit
sprite is; with the ground last it paints over everything below its own far edge at 0.50 and clips the
bottom third of the rock.
The rock band is at 1.00, the same rate as the ground, and that is geometry rather than taste: it shares a
contact line with a rigid texture scrolling at 1.00, and any other value slides the floor out from under
it. Parallax comes from the layers that touch nothing -- far at 0.30 across the basin, clouds at 0.15,
sky at 0.05.
The band's height_ratio includes its contact shadow, so its bottom edge sits below where the rock stands:
the feet are at 0.66, on the top line of the belt band, and the shadow fades out by 0.688.
The rock band is separated masses over transparency rather than a continuous run, so the floor shows
through between them and the two planes read as one piece of ground. That is also why far sits at 0.520
rather than 0.480: its own bottom edge has to be overlapped by the ground layer, and with the gaps open a
strip of bare sky showed through between them across the whole width.
The rock band is one continuous opaque mass -- rocks packed against and on top of each other -- with a
jagged top silhouette and a bottom edge made of the rocks' own feet. Continuity is what makes it
impossible for anything in it to float; the scalloped bottom edge is what makes the rocks read as resting
on the road rather than standing on a shelf.
Its content is graded by depth: small loose stones along the bottom where it meets the road, boulders
through the middle, big pale outcrops along the top, with the linework lightening and the colour cooling
as it recedes. That grading is what lets the band be this tall without the rock dwarfing the units -- the
near stones set the scale against a 122px unit sprite, and the large masses read as distant landforms.
The other three numbers follow from it and are measured, not chosen: the floor's own far edge is a
straight line that only the rock hides, so it has to sit inside the window the rock covers on every
column (0.391 to 0.591 here, so the floor is 0.510 with its edge at 0.490), and the far band has to reach
below that edge or bare sky shows between them, hence its base at 0.540. Re-measure all three whenever the
rock band is regenerated.
